paragraphs: Forecasting events in continuous time means predicting sequences whose events need not fall on a regular schedule. Standard neural temporal point process models predict one event at a time. Although this can capture the next event well, long forecasts repeatedly build on earlier predictions, allowing errors to accumulate.

ADD-THIN approaches the problem through a probabilistic denoising diffusion model that operates on whole event sequences. This changes the unit of modeling from an individual next event to an entire sequence. A central contribution is accommodating discrete and continuous information together: event sequences involve both distinct events and their positions in continuous time.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report density estimation performance matching leading temporal point process models, alongside substantially better forecasting. These findings distinguish two abilities: describing how likely an observed sequence is and predicting a future sequence. The reported improvement concerns forecasting in particular, supporting whole-sequence diffusion as an alternative when repeated next-event prediction becomes problematic.
neurips-2023-add-and-thin-diffusion-for-.tldr: ADD-THIN models whole continuous-time event sequences with diffusion, matching leading density estimators and substantially improving forecasting in experiments.

paragraphs: Graph neural network pre-training uses unlabeled graphs to learn knowledge that can help later tasks. This paper challenges the assumption that simply supplying more graphs will improve those tasks. The authors observe that additional pre-training data do not necessarily produce better downstream performance, motivating more deliberate selection of what the model sees.

Their data-active graph pre-training framework, APT, connects a graph selector with a pre-training model. The selector considers properties of the graphs and the model's predictive uncertainty to choose representative, informative examples. Uncertainty provides feedback about how confident the model is in the available data, so selection responds to the model rather than remaining fixed.

The model then learns from selected new examples while attempting to retain knowledge from earlier ones. Repeated interaction between selection and learning produces a progressive pre-training process. Experiments show better downstream performance with fewer training examples and efficient pre-training. The finding supports selective data use in the evaluated settings; it does not establish that larger graph datasets are inherently harmful.
neurips-2023-better-with-less-a-data-act.tldr: APT iteratively selects informative graphs for pre-training, achieving better downstream performance with less training data in experiments.

paragraphs: Visual feedback can help interpret noisy or hidden information and support internally generated imagery. This paper investigates how such capabilities might emerge through learning. Its proposal is that feedforward and feedback pathways become aligned while each pursues its own objective, allowing the two directions of processing to support one another.

Feedback-Feedforward Alignment, or FFA, makes each pathway a computational route for assigning learning credit to the other. The authors demonstrate this joint optimization with classification and reconstruction on MNIST and CIFAR10. In these experiments, feedback acquires functions including denoising, resolving occlusion, hallucination, and imagination, connecting the alignment mechanism to several kinds of visual inference.

The method also repurposes the credit-assignment computation as a goal-directed feedback pathway. This alleviates the weight transport problem associated with traditional backpropagation and improves the proposed implementation's biological plausibility. The authors present FFA as a proof of concept for how cortical feedback could acquire flexible functions, rather than evidence that the brain necessarily uses this particular learning algorithm.
neurips-2023-brain-like-flexible-visual-.tldr: FFA aligns feedforward and feedback learning pathways, producing several flexible visual inference abilities in a biologically motivated proof of concept.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across multiple clients, whose datasets may differ substantially. Clients can train in parallel or participate sequentially. While parallel training has received substantial theoretical attention, this paper addresses the missing convergence analysis for sequential training when clients hold heterogeneous data. The central question is how reliably the sequential process approaches its optimization objective.

The authors establish convergence guarantees covering strongly convex, general convex, and nonconvex objectives. Their comparison gives sequential federated learning better guarantees than parallel federated learning on heterogeneous data. This advantage appears in the analysis both when every client participates and when only some clients participate, making participation pattern an explicit part of the result.

Experiments support the counterintuitive prediction that sequential training can outperform parallel training under extremely heterogeneous data in cross-device settings. The theoretical and empirical contributions therefore reinforce each other around data heterogeneity. Better convergence guarantees should be understood as an optimization result; the abstract does not equate them with universally faster elapsed training or superiority in every federated setting.
neurips-2023-convergence-analysis-of-seq.tldr: The paper establishes stronger convergence guarantees for sequential than parallel federated learning on heterogeneous data, supported by cross-device experiments.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an object held in a hand from one RGB image requires reasoning about the object and its interaction with the hand. The authors identify a representation problem in existing signed distance field approaches: their reliability near the target makes it difficult to encode local hand and object cues together.

DDF-HO instead represents shape through a directed distance field. A query specifies a three-dimensional ray by its starting point and direction. The field predicts whether the ray intersects the object and, if so, the distance to the target along that direction. Randomly sampled rays collect geometric information ranging from local details to broader structure.

The model combines a two-dimensional ray-based feature aggregation scheme with a three-dimensional hand-pose embedding that accounts for intersections. Together these features model hand-object interactions. On synthetic and real-world datasets, DDF-HO outperforms all evaluated baselines by large margins, with an improvement of about 80% reported for Chamfer Distance. The results support the proposed ray representation and combined image-and-pose information for the evaluated reconstruction task.
neurips-2023-ddf-ho-hand-held-object-rec.tldr: DDF-HO combines a ray-based shape representation with image and hand-pose features to improve single-image reconstruction of hand-held objects.

paragraphs: Population snapshots reveal how samples are distributed at particular times without identifying which earlier sample became which later one. Reconstructing the dynamics between widely separated snapshots is therefore difficult. The paper targets approaches whose inferred trajectories either omit stochastic behavior or constrain the possible motion too rigidly.

Deep Momentum Multi-Marginal Schrödinger Bridge, or DMSB, extends the Schrödinger Bridge framework into phase space, incorporating motion alongside position. It learns a smooth trajectory of distributions for a stochastic system while matching the observed position distributions at multiple times. This connects the snapshots through a distribution-level evolution that can account for randomness.

The computational method adapts Bregman iteration and extends iterative proportional fitting to phase space to handle high-dimensional trajectory inference efficiently. Experiments on synthetic data and a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset report substantial improvements over baselines. The method also reasonably reconstructs evolving velocity distributions from position snapshots when an underlying ground-truth velocity exists but is unavailable to the method. That result concerns the reported reconstruction setting, rather than universal recovery of hidden motion.
neurips-2023-deep-momentum-multi-margina.tldr: DMSB reconstructs stochastic population dynamics across snapshots by learning smooth distribution trajectories in a space that includes position and motion.

paragraphs: This paper studies examples that consist of a bag of instances and a set of possible labels. Exactly one candidate label is correct, but training does not identify it directly. The challenge is therefore twofold: combine the information within the bag and determine which candidate label describes the bag as a whole.

Existing approaches assign expanded candidate-label sets to individual instances and then aggregate their predictions. The authors argue that this can overlook information available at the bag level and make the final decision sensitive to negative instances. DEMIPL instead uses a disambiguation attention mechanism to combine the instances into one vector representing the entire bag.

A momentum-based disambiguation strategy then works to identify the correct label within the candidate set. This separates learning a useful bag representation from resolving label ambiguity while addressing both in one method. The authors also introduce a colorectal cancer classification dataset for this setting. Experiments on benchmarks and real-world data show DEMIPL outperforming the compared multi-instance partial-label and partial-label learning approaches.
neurips-2023-disambiguated-attention-emb.tldr: DEMIPL uses attention to represent an entire instance bag and a momentum-based strategy to resolve its ambiguous candidate labels.

paragraphs: Few-shot generative domain adaptation transfers an existing image generator to a new domain using only a few reference images. The desired outcome includes convincing images, diverse outputs, and consistency between corresponding source and target images. This paper adds an emphasis on retaining source knowledge and relating multiple learned domains.

Domain Re-Modulation, or DoRM, freezes the source generator and introduces new mapping and affine modules to learn target-domain attributes. The resulting changes in style space can be combined linearly. Adding several such modules enables generation across multiple domains and mixtures of domains, giving the architecture a concrete mechanism for the proposed memory and domain association.

The authors also introduce a similarity-based structure loss. During training, it aligns the target image's autocorrelation map with that of the corresponding source image, encouraging consistent internal structure across domains. Experiments report superior quantitative and qualitative results for both DoRM and this loss. The brain-inspired language motivates the design, while the demonstrated contribution is the generator architecture and its few-shot adaptation behavior.
neurips-2023-domain-re-modulation-for-fe.tldr: DoRM adapts a frozen generator through added domain modules, supporting diverse target-domain images and combinations of multiple domains.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can improve robustness by training models on deliberately perturbed inputs. In self-supervised learning, this must work without class labels. A common approach creates perturbations by maximizing the self-supervised training loss, but the authors observe that a higher loss does not always produce a useful adversarial example.

This problem is particularly pronounced for non-contrastive frameworks, which lack negative examples. The proposed method gives the perturbation a specific target. For each instance, it selects another example that is both similar and confusing, using entropy and similarity to guide the choice. It then perturbs the original instance toward that selected example.

The approach makes target selection part of generating useful challenges for training, rather than relying solely on untargeted loss maximization. On benchmark datasets, it yields substantial robustness improvements for non-contrastive self-supervised frameworks. Contrastive frameworks also improve, though by smaller, consistent amounts. These findings suggest that the usefulness of an adversarial training example depends on how it is constructed and on the self-supervised framework receiving it.
neurips-2023-effective-targeted-attacks-.tldr: Selecting similar, confusing targets for adversarial perturbations improves self-supervised robustness, especially in non-contrastive frameworks.

paragraphs: Contextual linear bandits involve choosing actions while learning which choices deliver higher rewards. Batched algorithms organize learning into groups of decisions, limiting how often policies are updated. Large action sets make existing elimination-based batched methods impractical, so this paper seeks an efficient approach that avoids having to manage explicit elimination across the action set.

The proposed algorithm uses soft elimination to reshape the action sets at each batch so that optimal or nearly optimal actions can be identified efficiently. Its access requirement is a linear optimization oracle: a procedure that optimizes a linear objective over the available actions. The method uses that operation to construct its policy.

For a horizon of T decisions, the authors prove a high-probability regret bound of roughly square root T, suppressing logarithmic factors, with O(log log T) batches, matching the batch-count lower bound. For linear bandits, they also obtain a gap-dependent bound roughly inverse in the smallest reward gap, with an optimal logarithmic number of batches. These are theoretical efficiency guarantees with explicitly probabilistic regret claims.
neurips-2023-efficient-batched-algorithm.tldr: Soft elimination enables efficient batched linear-bandit learning over large action sets using only a linear optimization oracle.

paragraphs: Multi-objective combinatorial optimization seeks good discrete solutions while balancing several goals. Neural heuristics have shown promise, but learning efficiently and producing strong solutions remain challenges. This paper proposes EMNH, which trains a shared starting model and then adapts it in a few steps to single-objective subproblems representing different objective tradeoffs.

During training, a multi-task architecture shares part of its structure so the meta-model can learn in parallel. A scaled symmetric sampling method for objective weight vectors stabilizes this process. These components address complementary needs: making shared training faster and improving how training explores the different weightings of the objectives.

For adaptation, a hierarchical procedure systematically handles the collection of subproblems. Experiments cover multi-objective traveling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and knapsack problems. EMNH outperforms the evaluated leading neural heuristics in solution quality and learning efficiency. It also produces solutions competitive with strong traditional heuristics while using substantially less time. The reported benefit is therefore both stronger learned search and a favorable quality-versus-time comparison on the tested problems.
neurips-2023-efficient-meta-neural-heuri.tldr: EMNH combines shared meta-training with fast hierarchical adaptation to solve multiple objective tradeoffs efficiently and with strong solution quality.

paragraphs: A learning system often returns one model, even when many different models predict nearly equally well. This can restrict domain experts who want to examine alternatives or impose practical requirements. The paper instead studies the Rashomon set: the collection of near-optimal models from which a user could choose.

The focus is sparse generalized additive models, which use a limited set of variables and combine their separate contributions. The authors approximate the Rashomon set with ellipsoids when the selected variables are fixed. They then use those ellipsoids to approximate sets associated with many different variable selections, creating a searchable representation of alternative good models.

This representation supports studying variable importance across the model class, locating models that satisfy user constraints such as monotonicity or direct edits, and examining abrupt changes in component functions. Experiments demonstrate that the approximations faithfully represent the relevant model sets and help solve these practical tasks. The contribution makes near-optimal alternatives available for interaction, rather than requiring expert preferences to fit the single model initially returned.
neurips-2023-exploring-and-interacting-w.tldr: Ellipsoidal approximations make sets of near-optimal sparse additive models searchable for expert constraints, variable importance, and model editing.

paragraphs: Reconstructing surfaces from multiple images can combine signed distance functions with differentiable rendering, avoiding direct three-dimensional supervision. However, existing approaches often require lengthy optimization for each scene. GenS addresses this bottleneck with an end-to-end model designed to transfer to new scenes rather than train a separate network for each one.

Its representation uses a generalized volume at multiple scales to encode scenes, aiming to retain fine detail alongside globally smooth surfaces. A multi-scale feature consistency objective compares views in a learned feature space. This helps when direct photometric agreement fails, while self-enhancement of the features improves matching and reduces ambiguity when information is aggregated.

GenS also uses a view contrast loss that transfers geometric knowledge from dense inputs to sparse inputs. This targets regions visible from only a few viewpoints. Benchmark experiments show generalization to new scenes and performance exceeding the compared leading methods, including methods trained with ground-truth depth. The findings support combining a transferable representation with explicit mechanisms for matching views and handling sparse coverage.
neurips-2023-gens-generalizable-neural-s.tldr: GenS learns transferable multi-scale scene representations and view-consistency objectives for detailed surface reconstruction on new scenes.

paragraphs: Diffusion models work naturally with continuous representations, while language consists of discrete tokens. This mismatch has complicated their use for text generation. The paper treats diffusion and pretrained language models as complementary components, using the language model to connect text with a continuous space where diffusion can operate.

The authors first use encoder-decoder language models to learn high-quality language autoencoders efficiently. The encoder supplies latent representations of text, and a continuous diffusion model is trained within that latent space. During generation, diffusion produces a continuous representation that the pretrained decoder converts into natural language. This gives each component a distinct role in the generation process.

The approach is evaluated for unconditional generation, class-conditioned generation, and sequence-to-sequence generation. Across multiple diverse datasets, the authors report significantly better effectiveness than previous diffusion language models. These findings support latent-space diffusion as a way to build on existing language-model capabilities. The reported comparison is specifically with earlier diffusion approaches, rather than a claim of superiority over every language generation method.
neurips-2023-latent-diffusion-for-langua.tldr: The method generates continuous language representations with diffusion and decodes them using a pretrained language model.

paragraphs: Adapter-based transfer can first learn small parameter modules across many tasks and then adapt them using a few examples from a new task. This paper investigates how choosing among those modules contributes to success. Multi-Head Routing, or MHR, selects and combines subsets of adapter parameters, providing finer control than selecting whole adapters.

MHR outperforms Polytropon with a comparable parameter budget. A variant that tunes only routing, MHR-z, remains competitive while updating very few parameters. The authors attribute the broader gains to better multi-task optimization, supported by high alignment between task gradients, rather than the previously proposed explanation centered on modular recombination and local adaptation.

Routing proves most useful during multi-task pre-training. Accordingly, MHR-μ discards routing afterward and fine-tunes the average pretrained adapter for each downstream task. This produces an effective single-adapter method. Training that average for a few additional steps on the multi-task data also supports zero-shot transfer, with reported gains of up to three percentage points in accuracy over the baselines.
neurips-2023-multi-head-adapter-routing-.tldr: Finer-grained adapter routing improves transfer chiefly through multi-task pre-training, enabling effective variants that later tune only routing or an averaged adapter.

paragraphs: A code-comment generator learns from many projects, but their conventions and examples can conflict. Training one model to fit everything may therefore compromise its output for a particular piece of code. Adacom addresses this local mismatch by adapting the generator when it encounters a target code sample.

The method first detects whether the model may perform poorly because of such a compromise. It then retrieves a few helpful training examples that have contradictory counterparts in the training data. Retraining on the helpful examples strengthens their influence and is intended to unlearn harmful influences, tailoring the generator to the current target.

Experiments span seven comment generators and four public datasets. The authors report average improvements of 14.9% in BLEU4, 12.2% in METEOR, and 7.4% in ROUGE-L. They also find adaptation per code sample cost-effective enough for on-the-fly use and successful on out-of-distribution code. Together, the results support targeted local retraining as a practical way to address conflicts hidden within globally trained comment generators.
neurips-2023-on-the-fly-adapting-code-su.tldr: Adacom improves code comments by detecting target-specific training conflicts and briefly retraining on selected helpful examples.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning estimates distributions of returns, providing information beyond an average reward. Some algorithms use estimated uncertainty to explore optimistically. This paper identifies a potential problem: using estimated variance in that way can bias the data an agent collects and interfere with convergence or performance.

The proposed method randomizes the risk criterion used to choose actions while retaining a risk-neutral objective. Thus, variation in how the agent evaluates return distributions guides exploration without changing the overall objective to a permanently risk-seeking or risk-averse one. The authors formalize the approach through a perturbed distributional Bellman optimality operator that distorts the risk measure.

They prove convergence and optimality using a weaker contraction property. Their theoretical results support avoiding the biased exploration problem and converging to an optimal return within the analyzed framework. Empirical evaluation across multiple environments, including 55 Atari games, shows improvements over the compared distribution-based algorithms. The contribution connects an exploration design with both mathematical guarantees and experimental evidence, while identifying why variance-driven optimism can sometimes mislead learning.
neurips-2023-pitfall-of-optimism-distrib.tldr: Randomizing action-selection risk criteria supports exploration while preserving a risk-neutral objective, with convergence guarantees and empirical gains.

paragraphs: Low-bit quantization can make image super-resolution models smaller and computationally cheaper, but it can also reduce reconstruction accuracy. The problem becomes especially severe at two to four bits. QuantSR addresses this tradeoff through changes to both how values are quantized and how the network is used during inference.

Its Redistribution-driven Learnable Quantizer addresses the loss of representational variety caused by quantization. An efficient redistribution design introduces additional information during forward and backward passes to improve what the quantized network can represent, while being inference-agnostic. This targets the representational effects of low precision rather than treating reduced numerical precision as a purely storage-related change.

A Depth-dynamic Quantized Architecture shares weights while allowing inference to trade accuracy against computational efficiency. Experiments report higher accuracy than existing leading quantized super-resolution networks together with competitive computational efficiency. Convolutional and Transformer versions further demonstrate the approach across two architecture families. These results support combining a learned quantizer with flexible inference to make low-bit super-resolution more useful in practice.
neurips-2023-quantsr-accurate-low-bit-qu.tldr: QuantSR combines learned redistribution-based quantization with adjustable network depth to improve the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in low-bit super-resolution.

paragraphs: Two datasets can differ in ways that matter differently to different learning models. R-divergence approaches distribution comparison from this model-dependent perspective. The question is whether the datasets should be regarded as coming from the same probability distribution when assessed through the behavior of a particular learning model.

The central intuition is that distributions are likely identical if their optimal hypothesis has the same expected risk on each. Risk expresses the loss associated with the model's predictions or decisions. To estimate a discrepancy from data, the method learns a minimum-risk hypothesis on the combined datasets and compares its empirical risks on the two datasets separately.

This makes the discrepancy sensitive to the model and its loss, rather than assessing data differences without that context. The authors report state-of-the-art test power across supervised and unsupervised tasks, supporting its ability to detect differences in the evaluated settings. They also apply R-divergence to training robust neural networks with noisy labels. The motivating equal-risk intuition remains a likelihood claim, not an unconditional proof that matching risks establish identical distributions.
neurips-2023-r-divergence-for-estimating.tldr: R-divergence compares datasets through the empirical risks of a model trained on their mixture, measuring distribution differences from the model's perspective.

paragraphs: This paper tackles mass-conserving partial differential equations by viewing their solutions as evolving probability distributions. Its scope includes time-dependent Fokker-Planck equations and Wasserstein gradient flows. The aim is a scalable method that avoids temporal and spatial discretization, which can make solving these equations difficult in high dimensions.

The key idea is self-consistency: a velocity field moves a probability distribution, and that resulting probability flow must agree with the equation defining the same velocity field. This produces a fixed-point condition. Rather than directly minimizing its residual with a neural representation, the authors develop an iterative formulation using a biased gradient estimator.

That choice bypasses substantial computational obstacles and performs strongly in the reported experiments. The method accurately recovers analytical solutions where these are available and outperforms alternatives in high-dimensional problems with less training time. Its significance lies in replacing a direct residual-minimization problem with a practical self-consistency iteration. The empirical success does not change the explicitly stated fact that the gradient estimator is biased.
neurips-2023-self-consistent-velocity-ma.tldr: Self-consistent velocity matching solves a broad class of mass-conserving PDEs through scalable probability-flow iterations without spatial or temporal discretization.

paragraphs: Contrastive regression learns representations that respect distances between numerical labels. This normally requires labeled examples, leaving unlabeled data unable to supply the same training signal. The paper extends the approach by recovering relative ordering among unlabeled samples, allowing those samples to contribute without knowing their exact target values.

The authors observe that a feature similarity matrix still contains information about relationships between samples. Spectral seriation uses that information to recover an ordinal ranking. Crucially, accurate recovery is conditional: the errors in the similarity information must remain within certain bounds. The recovered ranking then supplies relationships for contrastive learning on unlabeled examples.

Those same rankings can also supervise the model's predictions, providing an additional training signal beyond representation learning. The work combines theoretical guarantees with experiments on different datasets, showing that the method can surpass existing leading semi-supervised deep regression methods. Its practical appeal is extracting useful ordering information from unlabeled data, while its theory makes clear that recovery depends on the quality of the underlying similarity relationships.
neurips-2023-semi-supervised-contrastive.tldr: Recovered ordinal rankings let unlabeled samples support contrastive regression, with accurate ranking recovery guaranteed when similarity errors satisfy stated bounds.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders are widely used, but their theoretical behavior still raises open questions. This paper develops statistical guarantees using PAC-Bayesian theory. It addresses both reconstruction quality and how closely distributions produced by the model match the distribution that generated the input data.

The first contribution is a PAC-Bayesian bound for posterior distributions conditioned on individual samples from the data-generating distribution. This is the key ingredient used to derive generalization guarantees for reconstruction loss. Such guarantees connect reconstruction performance to behavior on the underlying data distribution, extending the analysis beyond the examples used to fit the model.

The authors also derive upper bounds on discrepancies between input and regenerated distributions, followed by Wasserstein-distance bounds comparing the input distribution with the VAE's generative distribution. These address distributional fidelity in addition to reconstruction error. The contribution is a set of mathematical controls on these quantities; an upper bound constrains possible discrepancy rather than asserting that a trained VAE necessarily reproduces the input distribution exactly.
neurips-2023-statistical-guarantees-for-.tldr: The paper develops PAC-Bayesian guarantees for VAE reconstruction and upper bounds on discrepancies between real and model-generated distributions.

paragraphs: Temporal tensor data describe relationships involving several kinds of objects over time. Fixed latent factors give each object an unchanging representation, which can miss how those relationships evolve. Streaming Factor Trajectory Learning, or SFTL, models changing factors while also accommodating observations that arrive continuously.

The method uses Gaussian processes to represent factor trajectories flexibly. To make their computation suitable for streaming, it converts those processes into a state-space prior through an equivalent stochastic differential equation. An online filtering algorithm then updates a decoupled running posterior over factor states whenever new data arrive, maintaining uncertainty about the evolving representations.

The decoupled structure also allows standard Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoothing to compute full trajectory posteriors in parallel without revisiting earlier observations. This connects immediate online updates with a broader estimate of how the factors evolved across time. Synthetic tasks and real-world applications demonstrate advantages for SFTL. The contribution therefore combines a flexible temporal representation with an inference procedure designed around streaming access to data.
neurips-2023-streaming-factor-trajectory.tldr: SFTL tracks evolving tensor factors with Gaussian-process trajectories and streaming state-space inference without revisiting past data.

paragraphs: This paper studies self-attention by treating token representations as interacting particles. The goal is to characterize the geometry that emerges as those interactions continue. Its analysis assumes weights that do not change with time, allowing the authors to examine the long-run behavior of a fixed attention-driven dynamical system.

Using techniques from dynamical systems and partial differential equations, the authors show that token particles tend to cluster toward particular limiting objects as time approaches infinity. Which kind of object emerges depends on the spectrum of the value matrix. Thus, the matrix used in the attention mechanism helps determine the eventual organization of representations.

In the one-dimensional case, the authors additionally prove that the self-attention matrix converges to a low-rank Boolean matrix. Together, these results mathematically support the empirical observation that leading tokens emerge during Transformer processing. The fixed-weight assumption, infinite-time behavior, and one-dimensional scope of the matrix result are essential to interpreting the claims; they describe specific mathematical dynamics rather than every finite Transformer computation.
neurips-2023-the-emergence-of-clusters-i.tldr: Under time-independent weights, self-attention dynamics form limiting token clusters whose structure depends on the value matrix's spectrum.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a Transformer respond to examples in its input without updating its parameters. This paper develops a statistical theory showing how Transformers can implement familiar learning algorithms within that process. The constructions cover least squares, ridge regression, Lasso, generalized linear models, and gradient descent for two-layer neural networks.

An efficient implementation of in-context gradient descent underlies these constructions. They have mild size bounds, can be learned from polynomially many pre-training sequences, and achieve near-optimal prediction on various analyzed input distributions. The authors then show how a single Transformer can select among base algorithms, or even different kinds of tasks, according to the input sequence without being explicitly told which to use.

Two constructed selection mechanisms test the problem before learning or validate alternatives afterward. The latter supports nearly Bayes-optimal performance for noisy linear models with mixed noise levels. Experiments also demonstrate algorithm selection in standard Transformer architectures. The results establish possible mechanisms and observed capabilities, rather than claiming that every pretrained Transformer necessarily implements these constructions.
neurips-2023-transformers-as-statisticia.tldr: The paper proves that Transformers can implement and select learning algorithms in context, with statistical guarantees and experimental support.
